Learning Objectives
Outline anatomic structures of the hip and groin at risk of athletic injury.
Discuss an appropriate workup for patients with athletic hip or groin injuries.
Review the surgical and nonsurgical management of athletic hip and groin injuries
General Considerations
Injuries to the hip and groin often result from the predisposing bony morphology of the hip
and sports that involve twisting and pivoting forces on the hip.
Athletic hip injuries often involve a combination of intra-articular bony, cartilaginous and
ligamentous pathology with extra-articular musculotendinous strain or tears.
Physical examination and appropriate imaging studies are key in accurately diagnosing hip
injuries.

Many athletic hip injuries can be managed nonsurgically. In recent decades, arthroscopic
techniques have greatly evolved to improve the outcomes of patients with an athletic hip
injury.
Labral Tears, Femoroacetabular Impingement Syndrome, and
Hip Instability
Pathophysiology
The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous structure attached to the periphery of the
acetabulum.
The labrum often is injured in combination with bony morphologic variants, including
femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) or acetabular dysplasia.
FAI is caused by cam morphology of the femoral head and/or pincer morphology of the
acetabulum. Abnormal contact between the acetabular rim and the femoral head and neck
junction leads to chondral and labral damage.
Acetabular dysplasia is a condition in which acetabular depth is insufficient, leading to
abnormal stress of the periphery of the acetabulum. These forces often lead to labral tears
and early-onset osteoarthritis.1

Pathophysiology
The labrum is a fibrocartilaginous structure that is confluent with the articular cartilage
of the acetabulum. It spans the acetabular rim and is bridged inferiorly by the transverse
acetabular ligament. The labrum has a well-defined blood supply, mostly from its
capsular side and is well innervated.2,3 Given this innervation, labral tears may lead to
pain and subsequent dysfunction. Labral tears are classified according to the Seldes
classification system as type 1, which is a separation at the chondrolabral junction, or
type 2, which involves multiple cleavage planes of various orientations and depths and is
more consistent with degenerative tears.4 Some labral tears display characteristics of
both types.
Labral tears of the hip often are associated with underlying bony structural factors that
increase the forces applied to the labral and chondrolabral junction. The most common

structural abnormalities associated with labral tears are FAI and acetabular dysplasia,
which often is associated with the clinical spectrum of hip instability.5-8
Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome (FAIS) is a dynamic condition predisposed by
abutment of the femoral and head junction with the acetabular rim. FAI morphology
generally is categorized as pincer impingement from prominence of the acetabular rim
or cam impingement from prominence at the femoral head and neck junction. Many
patients with FAIS have a combination of cam and pincer morphology.8,9
A summary of FAI, its clinical features, and diagnosis is provided in Resource 1. In the
dysplastic hip, insufficient bony supports lead to edge loading, in which excess loads are
placed on the acetabular rim, including the labrum and the chondral surface. Acetabular
dysplasia is associated with hip osteoarthritis. Although the hip joint typically is
considered an inherently concentric and stable joint, the concept of micro-instability of
the hip has evolved, with increased micromotion of the joint leading to chondrolabral
damage and pain.10,11 Acute, traumatic hip dislocations in sports are rare but have been
reported. These injuries require emergent management via reduction of the hip joint
and management of associated structural injuries, including fractures if present.12
Patient History
Patients with a labral injury associated with FAIS or hip instability may report a sudden onset
of pain after a twisting or pivoting injury; however, gradual onset of groin pain associated with
sports participation also is common.
Pain often is aggravated by deep flexion and internal rotation motions.
Intra-articular hip injuries typically are associated with pain about the anterior hip or groin.
Patients with hip dysplasia may present with symptoms similar to those of patients with FAIS.

Patient History
Intra-articular pain often is localized to the deep anterior hip and groin. Although many
patients refer to the lateral or posterior hip and pelvis as their hip, pain in these areas is

less common and directly related to intra-articular pathology. The C sign has been
described as a cupping of the hand over the anterolateral hip, gripping the thumb and
fingers in a manner that triangulates to the hip joint. The timing and acuity of hip joint
injuries may vary, with some patients describing a sudden onset of pain and other
patients reporting a gradual onset of symptoms with progressive worsening.13 Many
patients with FAIS or acetabular dysplasia report a history of recurrent hip injuries or
strains. In athletes, the culmination of bony morphology predisposing patients to FAIS in
combination with an acute injury to the hip or repetitive twisting, bending, or pivoting
motions may lead to injury to the acetabular labrum and the acetabular cartilage. FAIS
symptoms are aggravated by flexion, adduction, and internal rotation positions and by
twisting and pivoting activities. With prolonged duration of injury, compensatory
symptoms may present, including various muscular pains to the lateral hip, core, and
low back.
Symptoms of dysplasia overlap with those of intra-articular pathology, including deep
anterior hip pain aggravated by twisting motions or activities predisposing the hip to
extremes of motion, such as ballet, dancing, and figure skating.
Physical Examination
Physical examination of athletes with intra-articular injuries, including FAI and a labral tear,
often reveals decreased range of motion in flexion and internal rotation.
Associated extra-articular injuries can be identified via palpation of key bony and
musculotendinous landmarks and resisted activation of key muscle groups.
Special provocative tests, such as flexion, adduction, and internal rotation (FADIR) and flexion,
abduction, and external rotation, are helpful and should be compared with the results of the
uninjured hip. These maneuvers elicit anterior deep hip pain in patients with a labral injury,
FAIS, or dysplasia.

Physical Examination
Physical examination of the hip and pelvis begins with evaluation of a patient’s gait
pattern. Gait abnormalities often are more challenging to identify in young, healthy

athletes who may compensate quite well for an injured joint. A coxalgic (or antalgic) gait
results from decreased duration of the stance phase to avoid pressure on the injured
limb. In patients with abductor musculotendinous injuries, a Trendelenburg gait results
from inability of the gluteus medius and minimus muscles to hold the pelvis level,
resulting in a drop of the contralateral hemipelvis and a compensatory lurch of the spine
toward the affected hip. This described pattern may be subtle unless a full-thickness or
chronic abductor injury is present. Visual inspection of the hip may reveal ecchymosis
overlying bony landmarks, such as that observed with a hip pointer. Range of motion
should be measured in a systematic, reproducible manner and include hip flexion,
internal rotation, external rotation, adduction, and abduction.13,14
Measurement of range of motion can be most reliably accomplished with the patient in
the supine position while avoiding contribution from the pelvis or lumbosacral tilt.
Although range of motion may be diminished in all planes if the hip is injured, flexion
and internal rotation most often are affected in patients with intra-articular pathology,
including FAI and labral tears. Palpation of bony landmarks and musculotendinous
origins and insertions may reveal areas of tenderness and clarify the etiology of
associated symptoms.13
Special tests include the log roll test; Stinchfield test; impingement test (FADIR); posterior
impingement test (extension, abduction, external rotation); and Patrick or flexion,
abduction, and external rotation test. The log roll test creates a gentle rotational motion
of the femoral head in the acetabulum without straining the extra-articular structures of
the hip and is specific but not sensitive for intra-articular etiologies of pain. The
Stinchfield test creates anterior hip pain via a resisted straight leg raise and is positive in
patients with intra-articular pathology; however, this also may be confused with pain
originating from the hip flexor musculature.13 Although reference to their eponyms is
often made, clear communication of findings is best accomplished by describing the
maneuver and the location of any incited pain. Deep anterior hip pain with FADIR (the
impingement test) often indicates intra-articular pathology. Although this often is
associated with FAIS, other intra-articular abnormalities, such as synovitis, chondral
injury, loose bodies, infection, and arthrosis, may result in similar physical examination
findings.

A patient with an unstable or dysplastic hip may present with similar clinical examination
findings as a patient with FAIS. In addition, apprehension or pain may be noted in the
flexion, abduction, and external rotation position. If concern for hip instability exists,
care should be taken to assess the patient for conditions associated with general
ligamentous laxity as evaluated via the Beighton score. A passively externally rotated
limb also may demonstrate diminished recoil to neutral if released.11
Imaging Studies
Initial imaging studies of the hip include a well-centered AP radiograph.
Various lateral views of the hip can be obtained. A Dunn 45° lateral view is the most sensitive
radiographic view for identifying cam morphology of the femoral head. A false-profile view is
useful for identifying anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) morphology, anterior acetabular
coverage, and evaluating anterosuperior joint space narrowing.
Key radiographic measurements and findings include the lateral center edge (LCE) angle, alpha
angle, anterior center edge angle, acetabular crossover sign, posterior wall sign, Tönnis angle,
and Tönnis grade.
MRI aids in identifying chondrolabral injuries and musculotendinous disruptions.
Three-dimensional (3D) CT reconstruction images are a useful preoperative planning tool for
patients with FAI.
Ultrasonography has become a critical adjunct in the evaluation of hip joint injuries, specifically
for guidance during diagnostic injections.

Imaging Studies
Systematic evaluation of hip imaging studies can simplify an otherwise daunting task.
Plain radiographs are simple and cost effective and offer a great deal of information. A
well-centered AP view of the pelvis can be used to evaluate acetabular coverage, joint
arthrosis, and fractures. Measurements on an AP view are highly dependent on the
radiograph being well centered without excessive pelvic tilt or rotation. The LCE angle
measures lateral acetabular coverage. An LCE angle greater than 40° is consistent with
pincer impingement, and an LCE angle less than 20° is consistent with acetabular
dysplasia. Similarly, the anterior center edge angle is a measure of anterior acetabular

coverage. The Tönnis angle is a measure of the angle of inclination of the acetabular
sourcil relative to the horizontal plane. Each of these measurements provides partial
information about the 3D anatomy of the acetabulum. The acetabular crossover sign is
observed if the anterior and posterior walls cross on an AP radiograph, representing
acetabular retroversion. The posterior wall is defined as positive if a point at the center
of the femoral head appears lateral to the posterior wall of the acetabulum,
representing posterior acetabular under-coverage. On a lateral radiograph, femoral
head and neck morphology can be evaluated. Cam morphology is observed if the
femoral head and neck junction has a more convex contour, leading to diminished
femoral head and neck offset. The alpha angle is a method for quantifying this
asphericity, with angles greater than 55° typically associated with cam morphology.15
The morphology of the AIIS is best assessed on a false-profile radiograph. Prominent AIIS
morphology adjacent to the acetabular rim may contribute to subspine impingement.
Morphologic variants, including acetabular over-coverage, retroversion, AIIS prominence,
and femoral head and neck junction convexity predispose patients to FAIS and
associated chondrolabral injuries.15,16
MRI of the hip and pelvis often is necessary to identify chondral, labral, and
musculotendinous injuries, including tears and strains. MRI provides a great deal of
information and is best interpreted in the setting of a well-understood clinical
examination and differential diagnosis. MRI also can identify findings associated with
early arthrosis, including subchondral edema or cysts and chondral damage, which may
not be evident on radiographs. These are important to identify and may portend a
poorer clinical outcome after surgical management. Magnetic resonance arthrography
often is performed to improve visualization of intra-articular structures. With
improvements in magnetic resonance technology, many high-quality MRI scanners can
be used without arthrography to obtain excellent quality images of the hip.17,18
CT can be used to augment radiographs and MRI and improve understanding of
morphologic variants associated with FAI. Because this imaging modality subjects the
patient to additional radiation, the tool often is reserved for preoperative planning
rather than a routine diagnostic examination. 3D CT reconstruction images are helpful in
planning osteoplasty to correct impingement morphology.19

Ultrasonography has become a valuable adjunct in the diagnostic workup of hip and
pelvic injuries. In addition to its ability to identify musculotendinous injury joint effusions
in dynamic fashion, ultrasonography often is used to guide diagnostic injections to the
hip joint and adjacent to musculotendinous attachments. Injections may consist of local
anesthetic only for diagnostic purposes or may include corticosteroids to afford more
extended symptomatic relief.20
Management
(Video 1)
Initial management of most athletic injuries consists of focused physiotherapy, activity
modifications, and NSAIDs.
Ultrasonographic-guided injections have become an important adjunct in the management of
hip injuries by being diagnostic or therapeutic.
Open and arthroscopic approaches for the management of FAIS are accepted; however,
arthroscopic management has substantially increased in the past two decades.
Hip arthroscopy for the management of FAIS, including labral tears, has resulted in successful
outcomes overall and specifically in athletes.
Labral repair or focal débridement may result in improved symptoms, with most studies
favoring labral repair.21
Labral reconstruction is a treatment option for irreparable labral tears, resulting in
encouraging outcomes.
Adequate correction of bony impingement morphology is critical for successful management
of FAIS.
Capsular management and closure during hip arthroscopy are gaining acceptance, especially
in patients with borderline dysplastic acetabular morphology.

Management
Similar to most athletic injuries, hip injuries often can be managed via a combination of
focused physiotherapy, activity modifications, and NSAIDs. This process may be initiated
before the completion of a full diagnostic workup, and, in patients with less severe
injuries, may obviate the need for additional investigation if pain subsides.
Physiotherapy, including core strengthening and postural training, myofascial massage
and mobilization, and hip mobility, is important for patients with these injuries and
patients who require surgical treatment. Cianci et al22 reported that, among adolescents
with labral tears, those with associated FAI morphology were more likely to require
surgical treatment. Lynch et al23 developed consensus-based best-practice guidelines for
the nonsurgical and surgical management of FAIS.

Ultrasonographic-guided injections have become a valuable tool in the evaluation and
management of injures of the hip and pelvis because they often are diagnostic and
therapeutic.20 Injections to most sites can be administered solely via local anesthetic for
diagnostic purposes; however, the addition of corticosteroid may afford more prolonged
pain relief. Some patients with milder structural pathology may ultimately not require
additional treatment via surgery. Value exists in attempting such nonsurgical treatment
measures even if surgical treatment is ultimately required. This allows for preoperative
optimization of joint mobility and hip and pelvic musculature and a successful
postoperative course. In addition, knowledge that all nonsurgical treatment options
were exhausted before proceeding with surgical treatment may boost patient
confidence.
Open and arthroscopic management of FAI is associated with successful outcomes.24
Hip arthroscopy has become increasingly more common in the past two decades.25
Techniques for safe access to the hip joint have been described with patients in the
supine position or lateral decubitus position.26,27 Adequate correction of impinging bony
morphology is important in addition to management of labral tears. As the concept of
FAI continues to evolve, the importance of thorough correction of bony impingement
morphology has proven critical to successful outcomes. Residual impingement
morphology has been cited as one of the most common factors leading to failed hip
arthroscopy and the need for revision surgery.28 Cam morphology is a 3D process, and
verification of resection via a combination of direct arthroscopic visualization and
fluoroscopic imaging, with views in varying degrees of flexion and rotation of the hip,
may help ensure thorough correction.29 Intraoperative dynamic assessment of the hip
to identify areas of impingement also has been advocated.30
Labral débridement and labral repair have been described, with labral repair gaining
increased support as an increasing number of series report favorable outcomes. Menge
et al31 reported on a cohort of patients with a minimum 10-year follow-up after hip
arthroscopy. Patients who did not require total hip arthroplasty during the follow-up
period after arthroscopic labral débridement or labral repair had considerable
improvements in patient-reported outcome measures, with no substantial differences
reported between the groups. Higher rates of conversion to THA were reported in
patients who were older, required acetabular microfracture, or had less than or equal to

reported improved outcomes in patients who underwent labral repair compared with
labral débridement at a mean follow-up of 3.5 years. A 7-year follow-up study by the
same group demonstrated similar results33 A prospective trial by May et al34 compared
42 patients treated via labral débridement and 145 patients treated via labral repair (66
with mattress-type repair and 79 with loop-type repair). No considerable differences
were noted between the patients treated via débridement or repair, and no differences
were noted between repair types. A 2014 systematic review by Ayeni et al36 identified
younger age, male sex, lower body mass index, a Tönnis grade of 0, and pain relief from
a preoperative intra-articular injection as factors more likely to be associated with
positive outcomes after hip arthroscopy for the management of FAI.
Labral augmentation and reconstruction have been used to manage irreparable tears. In
a 2016 systematic review that included 20 studies, Forster-Horvath et al37 reported that
labral débridement and labral reconstruction were associated with comparable results.
A systematic review by Rahl et al,38 which included eight studies and 537 hips, reported
clinically important improvements in patient-reported outcomes after labral
reconstruction, with no difference noted based on the type of graft used. In a study with
a minimum of follow-up of 5 years, Domb et al39 reported considerable improvement in
patient-reported outcomes, which were comparable with those of a matched cohort of
patients who underwent labral repair; however, the patients who underwent labral
reconstruction reported lower patient satisfaction at final follow-up compared with
those who underwent labral repair.
Outcomes of hip arthroscopy in athletes universally are positive. Several series have
reported successful outcomes in athletes who participate in various sports.40-45 Byrd et
al46 reported on a cohort of 62 active-duty military personnel with follow-up ranging
from 2 to 10 years. In that study, 94% of patients demonstrated improved symptoms,
with a mean modified Harris hip score improvement of 22 points, and 80% of patients
returned to active duty at a mean of 5 months postoperatively.
Labral repair techniques involve mattress-type labral base fixation or circumferential
loop stitch around the labrum. Neither technique has been shown to be superior to the

Greater Trochanteric Pain Syndrome
Pathophysiology
Causes of lateral hip pain often are grouped together as greater trochanteric pain syndrome
(GTPS) and may include pathology such as trochanteric bursitis and gluteus medius or gluteus
minimus tears.
Bursitis is not observed on the advanced imaging studies of many patients with GTPS.
Increasing evidence show biomechanical rationales for GTPS rather than an inflammatory
process rationale; therefore, the term GTPS may be more generalized but likely is more
accurate.

Pathophysiology
GTPS encompasses various etiologies of lateral hip pain, including trochanteric bursitis,
tears or enthesopathy of the gluteus medius and minimus, friction of the iliotibial band
over the greater trochanter, and often a combination of these issues.54 GTPS typically
presents as pain or reproducible tenderness over the greater trochanter, buttock, or
lateral thigh and is relatively common, affecting 10% to 25% of the general population.55
A retrospective study of the ultrasonographic images of 877 patients with GTPS revealed
evidence of bursitis in only 20.2% (177 patients). Of the remainder of the patients, 49.9%
(438 patients) had gluteal tendinosis, 0.5% (4 patients) had gluteal tendon tears, and
28.5% (250 patients) had iliotibial band thickening.56

Increasing evidence shows an association between abnormal biomechanics and GTPS. A
2015 study of 203 hip MRIs revealed a substantial association between increased
acetabular anteversion and gluteal tendinosis. The mean acetabular version in patients
with gluteal tendinosis was 18.4° compared with 15.7° in patients without gluteal
pathology.57
Several muscles insert at or near the greater trochanter of the femur, including the
gluteus medius and minimus, piriformis, obturator internus, and obturator externus.
The gluteus maximus has a broad origin from the ilium and sacrum and inserts on the
iliotibial band and the gluteal tuberosity of the lateral femur. The gluteus medius and
minimus lie deep to the gluteus maximus, originating from the ilium and inserting at the
greater trochanter. The tensor fascia latae originates from the iliac crest and inserts on
the iliotibial tract. Several bursae surround the greater trochanter to protect it from the
surrounding tendons. The subgluteus medius bursa lies superior to the greater
trochanter, deep to the gluteus medius. The subgluteus maximus bursa lies between the
gluteus maximus and the gluteus medius and lateral to the greater trochanter. A division
of this bursa commonly is referred to as the trochanteric bursa.58,59 Resource 2 reviews
GTPS and other extra-articular hip disorders.
Patient History
Lateral hip pain is the key finding in patients with GTPS.
Most patients with GTPS do not report a traumatic injury.
GTPS is predominantly diagnosed in females.
Pain from GTPS may confer substantial levels of disability and affect quality of life.

Patient History
Patients with GTPS typically present with hip pain. A careful patient history can help
differentiate GTPS from pain originating from the lumbar spine or groin pain originating
from intra-articular hip pathology. Patients often report difficulty sleeping on the
affected side and pain with increased periods of standing on the limb or with walking.

Pain can radiate down the lateral thigh to the knee. A dermatomal distribution of pain or
pain radiation distal to the knee should indicate the evaluation of lumbar spine
radiculopathy.54 Female sex is strongly associated with GTPS, with a fivefold increase
compared with males.60 A prospective cohort study of women treated for GTPS
compared with an asymptomatic control group reported that a lower femoral neck-shaft
angle and adiposity were associated with GTPS.61
Pain from GTPS may cause substantial disability and, if chronic, may affect mental
health, employment, and quality of life. A study found that patients with GTPS were the
least likely to be working full-time compared with patients with end-stage hip
osteoarthritis and asymptomatic control patients. Otherwise, GTPS appeared to confer
levels of disability and affect quality of life in a manner similar to that of end-stage hip
osteoarthritis.62
Physical Examination
Physical examination commonly reveals tenderness at the greater trochanter and surrounding
soft tissues.
Pain with resisted abduction may be noted.
In patients with a higher grade gluteus medius or minimus tear, a Trendelenburg sign or gait
may be observed.

Physical Examination
Physical examination often reveals tenderness with palpation of the greater trochanter.
Patients may present with an antalgic gait or the classic Trendelenburg gait if weakness
of the gluteus medius is pronounced. Manual muscle testing of the gluteus medius often
reveals weakness and reproduces pain at the greater trochanter. A physical examination
finding called the hip lag sign , in which the examiner places the hip in 10° of extension,
maximal abduction, and internal rotation, has been described. The patient’s inability to

actively maintain the position, with a noted drop of 10 cm at the foot, is considered a
positive finding associated with hip abductor damage substantiated via MRI.63
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs in patients with GTPS often appear normal but may demonstrate surface
irregularities or enthesophytes at the greater trochanter.
MRI is useful in diagnosing full-thickness and partial-thickness gluteus medius and gluteus
minimus tears.
Ultrasonography is emerging as a useful imaging modality for the diagnosis of gluteal tendon
tears and can be used to help guide diagnostic or therapeutic injections.

Imaging Studies
Radiographs of the hip may demonstrate surface irregularities at the greater trochanter
consistent with enthesopathy or calcific tendinosis. Radiographs also are useful in
identifying possible coexisting disorders, such as osteoarthritis of the hip and fractures.
MRI can depict osseous and soft-tissue abnormalities, including peri-trochanteric edema
and tendinosis or gluteus medius and gluteus minimus tears. The use of
ultrasonography to aid in the diagnosis and management of gluteal tendon tears has
evolved because of its low cost, availability, and ability to guide management, such as
anesthetic and corticosteroid injections.64 A systematic review that compared the
accuracy of ultrasonography and MRI in diagnosing gluteal tendon pathology with the
accuracy of surgical findings of the same pathology found that MRI was associated with a
sensitivity of 33% to 100%, a specificity of 92% to 100%, and a positive predictive value of
71% to 100%, with a high rate of false-positive results. Ultrasonography was associated
with a sensitivity of 79% to 100% and a positive predictive value of 95% to 100%.65
Management
Endoscopic approaches to the peri-trochanteric space allow for repair of gluteus medius and
minimus tears with outcomes comparable to those of open techniques.

Open repair techniques are associated with increased complication rates compared with
endoscopic approaches.
Iliotibial band–sparing approaches and trans-iliotibial band approaches have been described.
The iliotibial band–splitting approach may confer greater improvement in patient-reported
outcome measures and a decreased surgical failure rate.

Management
Most patients with GTPS can be successfully treated nonsurgically via rest; activity
modifications; NSAIDs; and directed physiotherapy, including massage/myofascial
mobilization. Peri-trochanteric injections may afford relief of symptoms and can be
performed with or without image guidance.54
In patients with recalcitrant pain who have a partial- or full-thickness tear of the
abductor tendons, repair of the abductor tendons can be performed.66 Various
techniques can be used to repair the tendons to their insertion, including open
transosseous or bone-anchored suture techniques, endoscopic techniques, and tendon
augmentation for repair reinforcement.67 Double-row fixation analogous to rotator cuff
repair has been described.68 A retrospective review of 12 patients who underwent
endoscopic gluteus medius tendon repair via an iliotibial band–sparing approach
showed improvement in International Hip Outcome Tool scores in 92% of patients
(mean 52-point improvement) at a follow-up of 2 years. All the patients in this study were
female.69 Another series of 15 patients treated via endoscopic repair showed
improvements in all hip-specific outcome measures at a follow-up of 2 years.68 A
systematic review of endoscopic versus open gluteus medius repair showed similar
outcomes between the techniques; however, the open repair group had more

The anterior bony pelvis, with its many muscle attachments and the pubic symphysis,

The layers, from superficial to deep, are the fascia, external oblique fascia and muscle,

abdominis fascia), and external oblique muscle merge to form the public aponeurosis,
which inserts onto the pubic tubercle. The medial thigh compartment consists of the
pectineus; the gracilis; and the adductor brevis, longus, and magnus muscles. The
ligamentous complex at the pubic symphysis consists of the anterior, superior, posterior,
and arcuate ligaments. The superior and arcuate ligaments are the main stabilizers of
the pubic symphysis.95

Athletic pubalgia is defined as an injury to one of the previously described structures,
because it inserts into the pubis, in a patient without a clinically recognizable hernia. The
term sports hernia is a misnomer, and core muscle injury currently is the generally

clinical examination results. Administering an intra-articular injection of local anesthetic
into the hip joint may be useful before having the athlete perform activities that typically
provoke pain or reexamining the patient in the office. Persistent pain in the groin or
lower abdominal region after intra-articular injection may be consistent with
concomitant or isolated core muscle injury. Anesthetic injection into the pubic
symphysis, adductor cleft, or psoas bursa also may aid in diagnosis.98
Management
Most patients with a core muscle injury can be treated nonsurgically via rest and activity
modifications.
Management of associated structural pathology, such as FAI, often improves core muscle
injury symptoms.
Multiple surgical techniques have been described for the management of core muscle injury,
including repair of lower abdominal muscular/fascial structures and release of the adductor
longus.
Surgical management of core muscle injury should be performed by an experienced surgeon
with expertise in groin pathology.

Pathophysiology
Myotendinous injuries and strains are more common if the muscle crosses two joints
and usually result from eccentric contraction.116 The injury usually occurs at the
myotendinous junction. Adductor injures often occur at the origin onto the pelvis and
may be caused by a mechanism of injury different than that associated with a typical
muscle strain.117 Adductor strains are common in athletes who participate in pivoting
and cutting activities and in kicking in soccer. The adductor group works in combination
with the abdominal musculature to stabilize the pelvis during walking and running.118
The adductor longus origin on the pelvis may be predisposed to injury because of its
small cross-sectional area compared with the size of the muscle belly.116 Another
etiology for adductor strain is a muscle imbalance between the abductors and the
adductors. Professional hockey players are 17 times more likely to incur an adductor
strain if their adductor strength is less than 80% of their abductor strength.116 A
considerable reduction in adductor strains in a similar patient population was reported if
a preventive adductor strengthening program was instituted.119,120

Patients with an adductor strain present with medial groin pain.

Osteitis Pubis
Pathophysiology
Osteitis pubis is a noninfectious, noninflammatory stress injury of the para-symphyseal pubic
bones caused by increased forces on the anterior pelvis.
Osteitis pubis most commonly occurs in athletes who participate in sports that involve twisting
motions.

Pathophysiology
Osteitis pubis is thought to be a stress injury of the para-symphyseal pubic bones
secondary to increased strain on the anterior pelvis.125 Osteitis pubis is described
secondary to chronic overuse, resulting in a stress reaction adjacent to the pubic
symphysis, and later leads to symphyseal pathology.126 This was demonstrated in a
study of pubic rami bone biopsies in athletes in whom osteitis pubis was diagnosed.127
The specimens showed formation of new woven bone, osteoblasts, and
neovascularization, with an absence of inflammatory cells and no signs of osteonecrosis.
Osteitis pubis commonly occurs in athletes who participate in soccer, Australian-rules
football, rugby, ice hockey, American football, and distance running.98
Patient History
Patients with osteitis pubis present with lower abdominal, groin, or anterior pelvis pain that is
aggravated by physical activity or direct pressure over the pubic symphysis.

Imaging Studies
The initial imaging modality for the evaluation of osteitis pubis is plain radiography. A
well-centered AP pelvis radiograph will appear normal in acute cases. Chronic osteitis
pubis (lasting more than 6 months) may present as cystic changes, sclerosis, or widening
of the symphysis. A single-leg stance AP flamingo view of the pelvis can be obtained to
evaluate for public instability. Widening greater than 7 mm or vertical shift greater than 2
mm indicates instability at the pubic symphysis.130 Radiographs also should be
evaluated for FAI, stress fractures, and avulsion injuries.115
MRI will show subchondral bone marrow edema similar to that observed with
osteoarthritis of other joints. The edema usually is bilateral but often will be asymmetric,
with increased signal intensity on the more symptomatic side. The bone marrow edema
will encompass the entire subchondral region of the symphysis from anterior to
posterior, differentiating it from isolated edema related to an avulsion injury.
Subchondral cysts and resorption of the subchondral bone also may be observed on
MRI.104 A severe episode of osteitis pubis may appear as articular erosion in addition to
subchondral edema similar to that observed in patients with osteolysis at the
acromioclavicular joint. Healing may be protracted in these more advanced cases.98,131
Management
Osteitis pubis typically is managed nonsurgically via rest, activity modifications, and NSAIDs.
Fluoroscopic- or ultrasonographic-guided injections of the pubic symphysis may alleviate
symptoms of osteitis pubis.
Surgical techniques, including curettage, resection, or arthrodesis of the symphysis, have been
described.
Management of associated intra-articular pathology, including FAI may result in resolution of
osteitis pubis symptoms.
